label: African history: postwar institutional expansion
date_label: Older traditions · Ibadan · Dar es Salaam · expansion from the 1950s · coverage through 2000
scope_note: The node concerns postwar institutions, not the beginning of African historical knowledge. Nationalist, Marxist, oral, and other methods require distinct contexts. Ibadan, Dar es Salaam and UNESCO are distinct institutional settings. Earlier Yoruba writing, West African spoken knowledge, East African reconstruction, women’s histories and labor inquiry are not one nationalist programme. Northern Africa and further African intellectual traditions still require expansion.

label: Annales
date_label: 1929 onward · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Generations overlap and disagree. The founders’ exchange programme differs from Braudel’s duration, serial economic models and the 1988–1989 methodological reconsideration. Roster contexts include named resources, critics and collaborators, not a uniform membership list. Women’s history and Italian microstoria retain independent histories; their specific exchanges do not establish a single Annales origin.

label: Anthropology & ethnography
date_label: 1800s roots · Tylor 1871 · Boas 1896 · later revisions · coverage through 2000
scope_note: A selective teaching map of sociocultural anthropology and ethnography, not all anthropology. Evolutionary, historical, functional, structural, interpretive, feminist and critical inquiries overlap without forming a single succession. Chinese research, Māori scholarship and collaborative histories have distinct trajectories. These approaches and rosters neither establish exclusive membership nor turn anthropology into one transferable theory.

label: Anti-colonial histories
date_label: Earlier roots · 1930s–70s expansion · coverage through 2000
scope_note: James, Williams, Fanon, and Rodney make different arguments. Colonial subjects and liberation politics do not establish one school or Marxist identity. Césaire’s polemic and Cabral’s political theory add distinct questions; cultural struggle and economic explanation can interact. The present Caribbean/African selection does not exhaust anti-colonial historical writing in Asia or elsewhere. Naoroji adds one Indian precursor through a specific1901argument; his use of Mill distinguishes theoretical borrowing from acceptance of colonial policy.

label: Atlantic & diaspora histories
date_label: Earlier roots; 1960s–90s expansion · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Oceanic reconstruction, imperial history, regional social history and diaspora critique overlap without one origin. Forced and other migrations require distinct analysis. These selections broaden Caribbean and Iberian contexts while leaving substantial Indigenous, Latin American and non-Anglophone historiographies underrepresented.

label: West German historical social science / Sonderweg
date_label: Wehler · Kocka · 1960s–90s debates and extensions · coverage through 2000
scope_note: A teaching umbrella spanning a research programme, a contested German-path argument and critics. Historical social science is broader than Sonderweg; neither is synonymous with the later Historikerstreit. Long-term conditions are not inevitable causes of Nazism, and gender history broadens the programme without making all contributors doctrinal adherents. Innovation also coexisted with inherited teaching relationships and politically contested continuities across 1945; the 1998–1999 debate over historians’ Nazi pasts is a distinct episode.

label: Biography / life writing
date_label: Ancient roots · Strachey 1918 · Davis 1995 · crosses fields · coverage through 2000
scope_note: A genre and set of methods with ancient and varied roots, not inherently great-man history, psychohistory or microstoria. The selected roster combines earlier practices, modern historical work and critics. Davis’s comparison preserves religious and colonial differences; her imagined prologue is not historical testimony. Bourdieu questions narrated coherence without banning life histories; Levi emphasizes choices within constraints and investigates group formation. Biography can explain wider relations, but its scale and source gaps remain subjects of criticism. Non-European traditions and original translation witnesses require further research; the current selection is not exhaustive.

label: Black history
date_label: 1800s roots · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Independent scholarship, community education, publishing and collecting precede later academic recognition. Biography, national synthesis and Black women’s history pursue different questions. This selection remains weighted toward African American scholarship; diaspora links do not make all Black histories one national tradition.

label: Conceptual history / Begriffsgeschichte
date_label: Koselleck · 1960s–90s development · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Koselleck’s conceptual change and historical time differ from reconstructing a particular author’s intervention. Brunner, Conze and Koselleck’s editorial association does not imply identical methods or political commitments. Experience and expectation are formal research categories with variable contents; the proposed modern temporal transformation is neither a universal timetable nor a prediction of particular events.

label: Consumption & material culture
date_label: Earlier roots; 1980s–90s expansion · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Demand, taste, provisioning, commodities, and material objects are not one theory; gender and empire connect consumption to production. Commodity circulation, cultural biography and goods as communication are distinct questions. De Vries acknowledges conflicting household interests; feminist research does not reduce women to consumers. Much of this selection concerns Europe and the United States; Mintz’s colonial production connects regions but does not make the coverage global in every respect.

label: Contextual intellectual history / Cambridge School
date_label: 1960s onward · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Skinner’s interventions and Pocock’s political languages are related but not identical; the Cambridge School is narrower than all contextual interpretation. Public conventions constrain possible interventions; historical context is neither a complete causal deduction of a text nor recovery of a private intention without evidence. Later accounts dispute simple Laslett-to-Skinner founding narratives. Named philosophical resources are particular receptions, not school membership.

label: British cultural studies
date_label: Hoggart · Williams · Hall · CCCS 1964 · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Hoggart, Williams, Thompson and Hall have distinct trajectories. Birmingham is one institutional center; feminist, antiracist, ethnographic and media projects revise its questions. Culturalist/structuralist distinctions are debated, not successive closed schools. Contributors listed as theoretical resources are not thereby CCCS members. Exchanges with history do not make the fields identical.

label: New cultural history
date_label: 1970s–80s expansion · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Anthropological interpretation, historical representations, and class/cultural experience are distinct resources; culture does not arrive after material explanation ends.

label: Historical demography & history of the family
date_label: Henry · Cambridge Group · 1950s–70s expansion · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Family reconstitution and aggregate reconstruction differ from histories of childhood or family meanings; Henry, Annales, and Cambridge are not interchangeable. Household composition, marriage behavior, concepts of childhood and parental conduct are different objects of study. England and France are prominent in this selection; Chinese comparative research broadens the questions without representing all non-European family histories. Later institutional webpages are retrospective sources, not an extension beyond 2000.

label: Dependency / world-systems
date_label: 1960s–70s expansion · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Dependency theories, Rodney’s African history, and Wallerstein’s world-system are related but cannot share every incoming or outgoing claim. Structuralist precursors are not automatically Marxist dependentistas. Bambirra’s defense of one Marxist current is a situated intervention; neither it nor Wallerstein’s disputed definition of capitalism settles the umbrella’s boundaries.

label: Digital history
date_label: Earlier roots · selected publications 2003–2022; field chronology unresolved
scope_note: Bounded selection of projects, methods, public practice and critical reflection. No founding year, complete genealogy or comprehensive field review through 2026 is asserted.

label: Social facts & collective life
date_label: Division of Labour 1893 · Rules 1895 · Elementary Forms 1912 · later school · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Durkheim and selected collaborators, recipients and interlocutors, not a membership register. Collective explanation does not imply that all institutions are useful or all differentiation creates solidarity. Colonial-era categories and ethnographic generalizations remain claims to assess. Bloch’s engagement is selective; modernization and Bourdieu links still need more precise reception passages.

label: Economic history
date_label: 1800s roots · Economic History Society founded 1926 · multiple paradigms · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Distinguish the relevant historians, evidence, and mechanisms before claiming an influence. A subject shared with Annales or Marxism is not itself an explanation. Institutional approaches are not interchangeable, and consumption does not replace production. Household interests can conflict. Gerschenkron’s European comparison and Pomeranz’s Eurasian argument have distinct scales; neither is a universal development law. Furtado’s demand analysis and Novais’s structural criticism offer a Brazilian exchange, with primary-edition and numerical verification limits retained.

label: Political economy & economic theory
date_label: Smith 1776 · Ricardo 1817 · Mill 1848 · Marshall 1890 · later adaptations · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Classical political economy and neoclassical modelling have different chronologies; North’s later institutional revisions add another distinction. This selection foregrounds earlier resources for historical inquiry, not a complete history of twentieth-century economics. Mill’s institutional argument and Marshall’s qualified assumptions prevent a blanket equation of theory with timeless laws. Polanyi appears as a later critic of a specific classical account, extending the selection’s historical reception without turning it into a complete history of twentieth-century theory. Earlier resources remain central, now joined by selected twentieth-century historical uses: Furtado’s Keynes reference, Block/Somers’s Polanyi reception and Lipset’s Schumpeter definition. These do not constitute comprehensive coverage of modern economics. Mill’s property qualifications coexist with colonial and civilizational assumptions; Marx’s Wakefield critique also retains a settler frame. Naoroji adds an Indian appropriation of Mill, not a globally representative roster.

label: Environmental history
date_label: 1970s consolidation · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route. Crosby’s temperate-settler argument differs from Melville’s Mexican case; Gadgil and Guha’s resource conflicts differ from Grove’s conservation networks and Carruthers’s park politics. Cronon’s cultural account of wilderness does not deny nonhuman nature. The selection remains incomplete, especially in environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship. A bounded second-pass addition now compares Bullard and the Huggins collaboration; primary-excerpt, publisher-description and metadata limits remain distinct, and neither selection represents every community.

label: Historical epistemology
date_label: Bachelard 1938 · Canguilhem 1943, expanded 1966 · coverage through 2000
scope_note: The French Bachelard–Canguilhem route differs from Kuhn, sociology of knowledge, and a generic philosophy of history.

label: Ethnohistory
date_label: Earlier interdisciplinary work · Great Lakes–Ohio Valley project 1953 · Lurie 1961 · continuing regional programmes · coverage through 2000
scope_note: The field overlaps with Indigenous history but does not automatically confer Indigenous authority, community consent or decolonizing method. Claims research could serve governments as well as claimants. Indigenous authors appear here as qualified interlocutors and critics, not as members of an externally assigned school. Lurie herself disputes restricting the approach to particular peoples. The Americas dominate this initial selection; Vansina provides a comparison with African oral-tradition methodology, not proof that African history descends from US ethnohistory.

label: Frankfurt School / critical theory
date_label: 1920s roots · Benjamin · Adorno · Habermas · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Benjamin’s historical time, Horkheimer/Adorno’s critique of domination, and Habermas’s public sphere require individual attribution. Empirical projects, exile institutions, Freudian debates and feminist/public-sphere criticisms are distinguished. Roster critics and historians are not thereby Institute members.

label: Freudian psychoanalysis
date_label: 1890s onward; divergent later schools · coverage through 2000
scope_note: This is a tradition entry, not an individual Freud node. Clinical claims and normative sexual classifications are historically situated. Breuer treated Anna O.; Freud’s account is not an independent outcome audit. Klein, Anna Freud, Erikson, Lacan and feminist interpreters pursue divergent questions. Historical motive inference requires documentary criticism; neither clinical access nor a uniform Freudian school can be assumed. Primary readings here cover the Clark lectures and selected Group Psychology chapters, not Freud’s entire career.

label: Gender history
date_label: Earlier roots · 1980s–90s expansion · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Gender history is a distinct research field with competing explanations and methods. Women’s history remains independent and is not superseded. Racial formation and intersectional analysis have their own entries; connections express specific arguments rather than membership in a combined school. Historical differences of class, race, caste, place and sexuality remain integral questions within gender history.

label: Geography & environmental inquiry
date_label: 1800s roots · Marsh 1864 · Vidal 1903 · Sauer 1925 · later inquiries · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Vidal’s human geography and Marsh’s environmental inquiry are different resources; neither defines all later environmental history. This is a selective set of resources for historians, not a complete history of geography. Sauer and Leopold supply distinct approaches; national framing, ecological care and landscape morphology are not a single programme. Harvey and Massey disagree within critical inquiry; neither stands for the whole discipline. Colonial frameworks are investigated as historically situated practices with internal conflicts. This expanded selection still does not represent global geography comprehensively.

label: World / global / connected history
date_label: 1960s roots; 1990s growth · coverage through 2000
scope_note: World synthesis, comparative development, capitalism, and connected histories differ in units, scales, and explanatory assumptions.

label: Historical economics
date_label: Roscher’s programme 1843 · Schmoller’s methodological review 1883 · coverage through 2000
scope_note: German historical economics, British institutional history, and empirical price studies overlap without forming one school. Roscher’s earlier programme and Schmoller’s generation differ. Menger is shown as a critic, and Toynbee explicitly rejects exclusive reliance on historical investigation. National and civilizational categories in these texts are historical claims to examine, not a globally representative framework. Jones’s providential harmony and Hildebrand’s national-capacity judgments are not adopted as findings.

label: Comparative historical sociology
date_label: Comparative programmes · 1960s–90s · earlier resources · coverage through 2000
scope_note: A field of competing comparisons, not one state-centered theory. Cases range beyond Europe, but this selection is uneven and does not exhaust regional traditions. Cultural and institutional explanations can be combined; political outcomes are not inevitable stages.

label: Historicism & idealist philosophies of history
date_label: 1800s roots · Dilthey 1883 · Croce 1917 · Meinecke 1936 · Collingwood 1946 · coverage through 2000
scope_note: German historicism, Italian idealism, and Collingwood’s re-enactment are not one doctrine; neither is this Popper’s usage of historicism.

label: History Workshop movement
date_label: Ruskin College 1967 · journal 1976 · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Adult education, socialist research, feminist criticism, and linguistic debates interact; no single turn describes the whole movement. The Ruskin workshops, later itinerant meetings and journal are related institutions with distinct histories. Retrospective participant accounts supply evidence about earlier practice without extending this map beyond 2000.

label: Holocaust historiography
date_label: Earlier documentation; 1960s–90s debates · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Persecution, perpetrators, victims, representation, and memory coexist. Intentionalist/functionalist disputes do not exhaust the field or precede all survivor scholarship. Wartime documentation, daily-life inquiry and rescue research complicate a perpetrator-centered canon. Explanation of radicalization is not exculpation, and disagreement over representation is not equivalent to Holocaust denial. The selection does not cover every occupied country or persecuted population.

label: Identity histories
date_label: 1960s–80s expansion · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Hunt’s later teaching grouping, not a school with founders or a unified historical agent. Recovery, multicultural synthesis, category criticism and self-determination have different stakes. Earlier Black and women’s historiography retains independent roots; named critics do not reject every collective claim.

label: Indigenous history & decolonizing methods
date_label: Earlier examples 1615–1938; 1970s–90s growth · baseline through 2000; selected 2010 intervention
scope_note: A selective grouping of independently rooted Indigenous historical practices and decolonizing research, with Andean, Haudenosaunee, Ojibwe, Cree, Métis, Wendat, Māori, Osage, Native Hawaiian, Yukon and Australian examples. Earlier writing, community knowledge, academic historical scholarship and decolonizing methodology have different histories. Community historians, academic historians and outside collaborators have different positions. Neither anthropology nor European theory is their common origin; no selection stands for every nation or protocol. Membership is a contextual intellectual contribution, not a binary Indigenous-identity classification. Journal counts are venue-based publication proxies and cannot date the origins of these practices or identify Indigenous authorship. Academic Indigenous history includes documented collaborations with scholars working across historical, anthropological and geographical inquiries. Shared research subjects do not establish intellectual descent. Later source dates are separate from earlier events; only Leddy’s 2010 article is accepted here as a selected post-2000 intervention.

label: Intellectual history
date_label: Earlier histories of thought · Lovejoy 1936 · Skinner 1969 · plural programmes through the 1990s · coverage through 2000
scope_note: An enduring field with internal disagreements, not a single lineage from Lovejoy to contextualism. The existing Cambridge School and Conceptual history entries retain their specificity. Maruyama supplies one Japanese inquiry with explicit translation credit, not global representation or evidence of Cambridge influence. Social and cultural settings matter without reducing texts to reflections of social position. Women’s intellectual histories and African, Islamic, South Asian and Latin American traditions still need much fuller coverage.

label: Intersectional analysis
date_label: Earlier Black feminist roots · Crenshaw 1989 · Cohen 1997 · coverage through 2000
scope_note: An analytical approach with Black feminist and other intellectual and political roots, not a single school founded from nothing in 1989. Crenshaw’s legal critique and Cohen’s political intervention are distinct. Connections to gender, racial formation and queer history do not establish that every practitioner adopts this approach, or a direct Crenshaw–Omi/Winant borrowing.

label: Historical materialism
date_label: Marx’s preface 1859 · Capital I 1867 · later Marxists · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Marx’s historical materialism must be distinguished from the competing historical programmes of later Marxists. Neither Marx’s late qualification nor Engels’s acknowledgment of political effects cancels their stronger causal claims. Lukács, Luxemburg, Lenin, Althusser, Cohen and feminist reworkings offer distinct arguments; shared materialist resources do not establish one doctrine or a verified world chronology.

label: Labour history
date_label: Webbs 1894/1920 · Thompson 1963 · expanding comparative and feminist inquiries in the 1970s–1990s · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Institutional histories, Marxist cultural analysis, feminist inquiry and colonial labour studies coexist and disagree. Thompson’s work already contains a cultural reorientation; later gender analysis involves productive inheritance as well as criticism. This selection includes Britain, the United States, France, South Asia and Africa but does not constitute global coverage. Labour institutions and historical scholarship about them have different chronologies. Fuller Latin American, Caribbean, East Asian and Indigenous labour historiographies remain priorities.

label: Linguistic turn / poststructuralism
date_label: 1970s–90s reception · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Structural linguistics, discourse, deconstruction, and narrative theory differ. A historical concern with language alone does not identify a poststructuralist.

label: Biographical & literary traditions
date_label: Ancient roots · Carlyle’s On Heroes 1841 · Strachey 1918 · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Earlier roots and literary practices overlap with modern historical biography without forming one origin story. Plutarch is one ancient example; Johnson’s private lives precede Carlyle’s Heroes. Strachey names particular models and sources, and Woolf distinguishes his achievements and failures. Her English canon is not a universal history of biography. Translations and abridgments mediate the texts encountered here; named literary resources do not by themselves establish a school’s founding.

label: Marxist social history
date_label: Earlier roots · 1940s–60s expansion · coverage through 2000
scope_note: British Marxist social history is the focus, with selected Caribbean and imperial exchanges and earlier radical traditions. Party-group collaboration, independent journals, adult education and later feminist or linguistic debates are different formations. The rosters include external interlocutors and critics; neither membership nor a single theory of culture, class or historical change is implied.

label: Medical & health history
date_label: Earlier medical scholarship · social-medicine interventions 1930s · later social histories · coverage through 2000
scope_note: An enduring field with several programmes, not a school founded by the Society for the Social History of Medicine or its 1988 journal. Sigerist prevents a simple doctors-to-social-historians replacement story. Africa is represented by distinct projects, not a regional proxy. Asian, Latin American and Indigenous medical historiographies, clinical scholarship and histories of psychiatry require fuller treatment.

label: Memory studies
date_label: Older roots · 1980s–90s expansion · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Halbwachs’s social frameworks, Nora’s commemorative sites, and Samuel’s popular uses of the past are distinct projects. Communicative and cultural memory are the Assmann project’s distinctions, not a universal taxonomy. War mourning, Holocaust memorials and feminist subjectivity require different historical explanations; this selection remains weighted toward European debates. Jelin’s Argentina project adds a pre-2000 case beyond Europe; it does not represent all Latin American memory work.

label: Microhistory / everyday life
date_label: 1970s–80s expansion · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Italian microstoria and German Alltagsgeschichte have distinct origins and aims; scale alone is not membership in either project. Evidence, narrative and generalization remain contested within this umbrella. Kracauer is a retrospective comparison, not a claimed founder. González’s Mexican microhistoria is included as a distinct local-history project; shared terminology does not establish transmission from Italian or German programmes.

label: Military history
date_label: Earlier roots · Howard 1961 · Keegan 1976 · multiple paradigms · coverage through 2000
scope_note: A research field with overlapping objects, not one school or a progression that supersedes campaign history. Delbrück and strategic scholarship supply distinct resources; military historians also reinterpret and criticize them. Keegan’s restricted battle definition leaves much colonial and guerrilla experience outside its frame. European military-revolution debates extend to overseas encounters without representing the whole world’s military historiography. Bourke, Winter and Nell retain distinct questions about bodies, mourning and recognition. Scholarly collaboration, library work, editing and archival limits are part of the field’s production.

label: Modernization theory
date_label: 1950s–60s expansion · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Economic stages, communication and social dispositions, institutional differentiation, and democratization are distinct explanations. These contributors are not all historians, and the models do not form one inevitable path. Lipset explicitly denies automatic democratization, Huntington prioritizes institutional capacity, and Eisenstadt’s 2000 argument revises convergence assumptions. These differences do not erase hierarchical categories, Cold War purposes or disputed empirical claims in earlier models; a later program is not projected into every 1950s text.

label: Nationalism studies
date_label: Modernist debates · 1983 landmark works · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Anderson, Gellner, Hobsbawm, Smith, and Chatterjee supply competing accounts, not a common modernist theory. Hroch’s comparative phases, Billig’s everyday reminders and Yuval-Davis’s gender analysis address different questions. Nations, states and nationalist movements are not interchangeable; European typologies require testing beyond their original cases.

label: National & imperial narratives
date_label: 1800s–1900s · nation-building, empire and counter-histories · coverage through 2000
scope_note: A teaching umbrella, not a single national or imperial doctrine. Cultural and documentary inquiry coexist with narratives of progress. Colonial policy, anticolonial histories, subaltern criticism and collective African projects have different aims; no universal nationalist origin or automatic emancipation is implied.

label: New Left & radical history (US)
date_label: 1950s–70s expansion · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Radical diplomatic history, labour history, and slavery history differ. William Appleman Williams is not Eric Williams. This is a US teaching grouping, not the British New Left or a single party line. Collaborators and interlocutors are selected by particular work, without imputing all of an author’s later politics to it. Edited testimony, cultural analysis and quantitative resources can coexist.

label: Earlier cultural history
date_label: Burckhardt’s Renaissance 1860 · Huizinga’s Autumn 1919 · coverage through 2000
scope_note: A teaching grouping of distinct projects, not one school or an immature stage inevitably superseded by a cultural turn. National, social and cultural inquiry overlap. Period contrasts, elite claims, developmental rankings and the uneven survival of sources require scrutiny; collective psychology here is not psychoanalysis.

label: Oral history
date_label: 1940s institutions · expansion from the 1960s · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Recording testimony and interpreting the production of memory are related tasks; oral tradition and the life-history interview are distinct sources.

label: Explanation & objectivity debates
date_label: Earlier roots · Becker address 1931 · Hempel 1942 · Carr 1961 · Elton 1967 · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Covering laws, understanding action, historical facts, and objectivity are different disputes; participants do not form a shared school. Hempel’s probabilistic sketches, Dray’s challenge, Carr’s reciprocal research and Mink’s comprehension are distinct. Primary readings and publisher-only contexts are explicitly separated.

label: Political history
date_label: 1800s roots · Namier 1929 · Hunt 1984 · multiple paradigms · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

label: Postcolonial history / critique
date_label: 1970s roots · expansion from the 1980s · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Said, Spivak, and Chakrabarty address different problems; literary critique and historical scholarship interact without becoming the same discipline. Feminist critiques, colonial archival research and theories of ambivalence introduce further disagreements. These selections do not make postcolonial thought synonymous with South Asian history, literary theory or all anti-colonial politics.

label: Practice theory
date_label: Bourdieu · de Certeau · Sewell · 1970s–90s development · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Bourdieu, de Certeau, and Sewell offer distinct accounts. Practice theory is not a unified successor to cultural history. Collaborative everyday research, cultural repertoires and Ortner’s plural orientation broaden this selection. Strategy has different meanings across these authors.

label: Progressive & consensus historiography (US)
date_label: Contrasting frameworks prominent in the 1890s–1950s · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Progressive and consensus interpretations are contrasting positions. Attribute criticisms and economic explanations to the relevant side. Hofstadter’s critical portraits, Hartz’s fear of conformity and Boorstin’s appraisal must remain distinct. Frontier/free-land and civilizational hierarchies in older texts are historical claims, not this atlas’s categories.

label: Psychohistory / psychoanalytic history
date_label: Earlier roots; postwar growth · 1950s–80s · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Erikson, Gay and deMause have different explanatory ambitions; they are not interchangeable applications of Lacan. Schapiro’s art-historical criticism supplies a methodological interlocutor, not blanket rejection of psychoanalysis. Pollock’s thesis and deMause’s later response address distinct texts and disputed evidential procedures. Original case books and wider political, religious and regional applications remain selective research limits; theoretical or clinical assertions are not established diagnoses of past people.

label: Public history
date_label: Earlier public practices · US training discussions 1975 · The Public Historian 1978 · coverage through 2000
scope_note: The US professional programme is one formation. British local/oral practice and South African worker education enter as distinct interlocutors. Neither all public memory nor every popular historical product is equated with professional public history. Museum practice, Indigenous authority and non-Anglophone formations need fuller treatment.

label: Quantitative history
date_label: 1950s–70s expansion · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Serial history, demographic reconstruction, and cliometrics use numbers differently. A quantitative method does not establish a common theory. Counting, source linkage and formal modeling require different assumptions. Recorded categories, missing people and units of comparison shape conclusions; neither criticism nor narrative history ended quantitative research.

label: Sexuality & queer history
date_label: 1970s roots; 1990s turn · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Histories of sexuality, gay/lesbian recovery, queer theory and trans interventions overlap without a single succession or uniform Foucauldian position. Material explanation, interviewing, literary analysis and colonial research differ; historical practices do not automatically establish a timeless modern identity. Geographic coverage remains selective.

label: Racial formation
date_label: Earlier roots · Omi–Winant 1986 / revised 1994 · coverage through 2000
scope_note: A distinct theoretical programme relevant to histories of racialization, not a synonym for Black history or all scholarship about race. Original 1986 and revised 1994 editions remain distinct. The checked course extract is labelled second edition; its retyped pagination and edition attribution have not been independently authenticated. Intersectional analysis connects racial inquiry with gender, class and sexuality without being identical to racial-formation theory.

label: Critical historical scholarship
date_label: Earlier philological roots · Ranke’s preface 1824 · later archival scholarship · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Ranke is an exemplar within older critical practices. Archival scholarship is neither exclusively political nor simply positivist. Mabillon, Droysen and the French methodologists expose different practices and disagreements. Ranke’s theological and exclusionary claims are not atlas assumptions; critical inquiry has non-European histories beyond this selected European genealogy.

label: Revival of narrative / debate over quantification
date_label: Stone 1979 · Hobsbawm 1980 · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Stone’s diagnosis and Hobsbawm’s response concern historical practice. White’s prior analysis of narrative form is a different question. Stone’s own qualifications about plurality, evidence and continuing quantitative work accompany Hobsbawm’s criticism. Named examples do not imply the authors accepted Stone’s diagnosis.

label: Structural linguistics
date_label: Saussure’s Course, posthumous, 1916 · later linguistic programmes · coverage through 2000
scope_note: A selective teaching umbrella, not one uniform school or a claim that all linguistics descends from Saussure. The Course is posthumously reconstructed; Meillet’s social explanation, phonological programmes and Hjelmslev’s formal distinctions differ. Later reception is separately evidenced. Benveniste and broader linguistic traditions remain review gaps.

label: History of science
date_label: Earlier roots · History of Science Society founded 1924 · later approaches · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Kuhn is a central reorientation, not the field’s sole founder. Sarton, Koyré, Merton, and historians of experimental practice distinguish important approaches; Yates and Foucault are additional contributions. Chinese science and women’s scientific work expand this selection; it still needs fuller coverage of other regions and material practices. Named Chinese-series contributors and Daston/Galison’s image and instrument studies deepen the selection. Publication credits do not replace primary argument checks; wider regional coverage remains selective. Arabic mathematics, colonial Indian science, African healing and a Beninese knowledge programme are separate selected projects, not regional proxies or exhaustive coverage.

label: New social history
date_label: 1950s–70s expansion · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Class formation, demographic reconstruction, communities, and everyday life have different methods; Marxist history is one substantial component. The 1950s–1970s label marks expansion, not termination: later mapped works extend and dispute these programmes. Earlier women’s social inquiry remains visible as comparison. Neither one European class trajectory nor transparent experience supplies a universal model; critical interventions do not erase productive inheritances.

label: Spatial history / Historical geography
date_label: Sauer 1925 · Hoskins 1955 · critical spatial studies and historical GIS by the 1990s · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Historical geography has roots well before digital mapping. Spatial history is an overlapping set of approaches, not a synonym for GIS or one unified school. The existing Geography & environmental inquiry entry retains its wider intellectual resources. This selection foregrounds British reconstruction, Australian colonial space and a British HGIS project; wider regional traditions and Indigenous spatial knowledge require fuller treatment. Later digital projects are not backdated into coverage through 2000.

label: Sociology of scientific knowledge / SSK
date_label: Strong Programme · 1970s onward · coverage through 2000
scope_note: The strong programme and related sociology concern explanations of knowledge; they are not identical to all STS or laboratory ethnography.

label: Science and technology studies / STS
date_label: Interdisciplinary consolidation · 1970s–90s · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Sociological, ethnographic, technological, and policy-oriented projects interact. A discipline-level label cannot substitute for a named research programme.

label: Subaltern Studies
date_label: 1982 onward · coverage through 2000
scope_note: The collective changes across time; subordinate agency, colonial archives, and representation must not become a single unchanging postcolonial theory. Guha’s autonomy thesis, Spivak’s representation problem and Sarkar’s internal criticism are not interchangeable. Religion, gender, labor, local memory and colonial knowledge remain distinct questions; the present roster is geographically selective.

label: History of technology
date_label: Enduring field · SHOT 1958 · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Technical systems, use, household labour, and social change are different problems; the field has institutions distinct from history of science.

label: Historians’ responses to postmodernism
date_label: Plural reassessments · 1990s · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Defences, critiques, and revisions of historical knowledge conflict. A collection with White’s afterword cannot stand for unanimous rejection of him. Primary introductions distinguish skeptical interpretation, practical realism, disciplinary criticism and empirical reassessments. Exact source notes separate the editors’ descriptions of essays from reading the essays themselves.

label: Urban history
date_label: Earlier city histories · postwar expansion · Urban History Yearbook 1974 · coverage through 2000
scope_note: British institution-building and US quantitative urban studies do not define one school or exhaust the field. Cities are not self-contained units. Delhi adds a specific colonial inquiry; wider Asian, African, Latin American and medieval/early-modern historiographies remain underrepresented. Journal milestones mark consolidation, not the first historical study of cities.

label: Strategic & military scholarship
date_label: Earlier roots · Clausewitz’s On War 1832 · Delbrück’s volumes 1900–20 · coverage through 2000
scope_note: A selective teaching umbrella, weighted toward European and Anglophone scholarship, with a Chinese text and its mediated reception distinguished. Delbrück explicitly uses Ranke, Beloch and biographical research; these roots are not independent of every other historical tradition. Theory does not guarantee successful action. Marie’s editing and later translations are substantive mediation. Corbett writes for an imperial setting; neither that perspective nor Mahan’s national judgments is universalized. Bassford’s later online corrections are not assigned to his 1994 argument.

label: Web history / Archived-web research
date_label: Earlier roots · selected publications 2003–2026; field chronology unresolved
scope_note: Bounded selection of projects, methods, public practice and critical reflection. No founding year, complete genealogy or comprehensive field review through 2026 is asserted.

label: Interpretive historical sociology
date_label: Weber’s Protestant Ethic 1904–05 · later comparative inquiry · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Interpretive sociology, capitalist development, and theories of domination travel through different readers and intermediaries. Ideal types are analytical constructions, not averages or stages every society must traverse. Marianne Weber contributes independent legal-historical research and posthumous editing; Parsons and Lipset make particular later uses. Weber’s qualified defense of materialist inquiry prevents a simple Marx-versus-ideas binary.

label: Women’s history
date_label: Nineteenth-century and interwar work; renewed expansion from the 1960s · coverage through 2000
scope_note: Earlier documentary, economic and institutional projects overlap with later feminist reconstruction and theory. Periodization, class, race, caste and regional contexts create disagreements within women’s history. Gender history develops some of these questions without superseding the field; this roster remains selective and uneven geographically.
